In this post, we showcase a RAG application on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with LangChain. We run the same multi-part question through standard and agentic retrieval, and read the trace events to see the plan the model produced. We also cover what the two retrieval paths cost and when the cheaper one is the right choice.

Agentic retrieval is available on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Instead of one search, Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base plans the retrieval. It breaks the question into sub-queries, runs them, judges whether it has enough evidence, and searches again if it doesn’t. The `langchain-aws` package exposes both agentic and standard retrieval, so you can use either from a LangChain application.

The AgenticRetrieveStream API runs a planning loop and streams the steps back to you as trace events. Use Retrieve for short, well-scoped questions. It is cheaper, faster, works against self-managed knowledge bases, and returns scores in the results. Most production traffic looks like this.

# 1T MoE Quantization: ISTA SpTC on NVIDIA B200
...
- Hardware-software co-design for MoE models: Researchers present a joint quantization and sparsity system (reducing precision and unneeded weights) optimized for GPU Sparse Tensor Cores.
- Accuracy preserved up to 1 trillion parameters: The method maintains 96.09% of original model performance on one-trillion-parameter models, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques by 4.35 percentage points.

Although modern datacenter GPUs incorporate Sparse Tensor Cores (SpTCs)—hardware compute units designed to halve workloads by cutting superfluous calculations (known as sparsity) and compressing numbers to lower precision—truly leveraging them with MoE models has always proved difficult. Until now, applying these reductions led to noticeable drops in response quality and suffered from a lack of optimized software instructions. In a new technical study, researchers Kwanhee Lee, Namhoon Lee, and Dan Alistarh from ISTA introduced a joint hardware-software co-design approach: a method capable of compressing expert weights directly into the chip's native supported format, accelerating large-scale inference (text generation).
...
1. Coordinated mathematical optimization (continuous relaxation):
...
2. Custom chip instructions (grouped sparse GEMM kernel): At the low-level code layer, the team wrote a dedicated kernel (a program that directly drives GPU circuits) for grouped matrix multiplications (grouped sparse GEMM, the core mathematical operation of MoE models). The kernel is tailored specifically to interface with the sparse Tensor Cores of next-generation accelerators.
...
## Benchmarks and performance on NVIDIA B200

Laboratory validation evaluated MoE models ranging from 30 billion up to 1,000 billion parameters (one trillion). In terms of linguistic fidelity and reasoning, the framework minimizes the typical losses of compression: it surpasses the prior state of the art by a solid 4.35 percentage points, retaining an average of 96.09% of the original full-precision model's performance.

The most striking impacts, however, emerge during the serving phase (delivering actual responses to users). In tests conducted on the NVIDIA B200 chip, the researchers' optimized routine outperformed the vendor's official libraries:

- Raw kernel speed: Execution speed increased by up to 1.65× compared to standard software engines.
- Overall serving throughput: Total request throughput increased by 1.18×.
- Response times (end-to-end latency): A complete response arrives up to 4.03× faster compared to unoptimized processing.
...
By demonstrating that tight synergy between mathematical algorithms and physical silicon instructions can preserve over 96% of original quality even at trillion-parameter scale, the study by Lee and Alistarh marks a decisive milestone. Compressing and accelerating MoE models ceases to be a theoretical trade-off and becomes a practical lever for slashing energy costs and server expenses incurred by labs serving mixture-of-experts models.

signals.title: Tailoring the Quantization Space for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression · SyncAI.news
signals.excerpt:
Tailoring the Quantization Space for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression · SyncAI.news
...
# Tailoring the Quantization Space for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression

arXiv:2610.03027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache becomes a major memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference, placing substantial pressure on memory capacity and bandwidth. To mitigate this bottleneck, vector quantization (VQ) has emerged as a promising approach for aggressive KV cache compression. However, existing VQ methods degrade substantially in the 1-bit regime. At such extreme compression, each codebook must represent a larger group of channels with a limited set of centroids, making effective use of its capacity increasingly challenging. To address this, we introduce $\textbf{TaSQ}$, which tailors the VQ target space by combining query-guided channel weighting, cross-head normalization, and covariance-aware channel grouping to better reflect the error sensitivity and statistical structure of cached activations. Since these transforms are RoPE-compatible and can be easily merged into projection weights and codebooks, TaSQ preserves the conventional VQ lookup structure and adds negligible serving overhead. Across general, long-chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval benchmarks, TaSQ consistently outperforms existing low-bit KV cache VQ baselines while preserving reasoning stability. On a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU, its SGLang implementation supports up to $14\times$ larger batch sizes and achieves $1.87\times$ higher peak throughput compared to the BF16 baseline.

signals.title: Four Blackwell Formats, One Model: Quantizing Qwen3-32B on RTX PRO 6000
signals.excerpt:
Four Blackwell Formats, One Model: Quantizing Qwen3-32B on RTX PRO 6000
...
NVIDIA's Blackwell chips change that. Native 8-bit floating point isn't new: Hopper (H100) and Ada (L40S) GPUs already had FP8 tensor cores. What Blackwell adds is native FP4 (and FP6) math and hardware support for microscaling (MX) block formats, so 4-bit floating point runs natively instead of being faked in software. The lineup goes from the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition up to the data-center B200 / GB200 systems. This matters because on older hardware, quantization was mostly a way to make a model small enough to fit in memory — any speedup was a bonus, and usually a small one. On Blackwell, the low-bit formats run on dedicated hardware, so moving to FP8 or FP4 gives you real, measurable speed, not just less memory use.
...
What this article does. We take one model — Qwen3-32B — and quantize it into four Blackwell floating-point formats using AWQ: FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4 and MXFP4. We left out FP6 / MXFP6 and FP8 E5M2 (E5M2 is mainly used for gradients in training; inference checkpoints use E4M3). Then we measure two things that matter in production:

- Quality: Wikitext perplexity and GSM8K accuracy, to see what each format costs you.
- Serving performance: output throughput and time-to-first-token across a range of concurrency levels, to see what each format gives you under real load.

The result is a fair, side-by-side comparison of BF16, FP8-AWQ, MXFP8-AWQ, NVFP4-AWQ, and MXFP4-AWQ on the same hardware — boiled down to three charts and one table you can act on. The rest of this post walks through both sides, starting with a short look at how the quantization works. For a deeper theoretical and hands-on introduction, see our earlier post, The vLLM Quantization Complete Guide + Benchmarks. It covers the well-known algorithms, including AWQ, GPTQ, BitsAndBytes, TorchAO, Marlin-AWQ, Marlin-GPTQ, BitBLAS and ModelOPT.
...
- MXFP4-AWQ — microscaling applied to a 4-bit float (E2M1: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa — only ~8 distinct magnitudes). Each 32-value block shares one power-of-two scale. This shrinks the weights about 3.3× (18.59 GiB vs 61.03 GiB), but with only a single mantissa bit per weight it takes a real quality hit. In our run it also did not use Blackwell's FP4 tensor cores: it ran on vLLM's Marlin weight-only kernel with BF16 activations (see the serving flags in the setup), so its speed here reflects that fallback kernel, not the MXFP4 format.
...
is large as NVFP4 is about 3.1× smaller than BF16 (19.55 GiB vs 61.03 GiB; the scale factors add bits and some layers stay in BF16), and on Blackwell the native 4-bit tensor cores make it the fastest format we tested — for only a modest
...
We have compressed Qwen3-32B into all four formats and published the checkpoints on Hugging Face:
...
- Model: Qwen3-32B
- Hardware: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition
- Software: vLLM 0.24.0, lm-eval 0.4.12, compressed-tensors 0.17.0
- Accuracy benchmarks: Wikitext perplexity (word PPL, WikiText-2 test split) and GSM8K (strict / flex) on the first 100 of the 1,319 test questions
- Serving benchmark: ShareGPT V3, 1000 prompts, all sent at once (`--request-rate inf`), single run per concurrency level
- Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20 (Qwen3 defaults), EOS stopping on
- Client / server: `vllm bench serve` / `vllm serve` (vLLM)
- Max model length: 4096
- GPU memory utilization: 0.90
- KV cache capacity (tokens): BF16 93,312 · FP8 212,864 · MXFP8 208,192 · NVFP4 264,272 · MXFP4 267,200
- Prefix caching: on. One server handled the whole concurrency sweep with the same seeded prompts, so by the end the prefix cache hit rate was 0% for BF16, ~8% for FP8 and MXFP8, and ~14% for NVFP4 and MXFP4. This gives the quantized models a small extra boost.
- Quantization: calibration with 512 samples × 2048 tokens from the WikiText-2 train split, sharded across two GPUs (it ran out of memory on one). Perplexity is also measured on WikiText-2 (test split), so the same kind of text may make perplexity look a bit better than it would elsewhere.
...
Serving flags. Two of the variants needed an extra environment flag on `vllm serve` to run correctly on this hardware; the other two ran with defaults:

| Variant | Extra flag on `vllm serve` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MXFP8-AWQ | (none) | Runs with defaults |
| NVFP4-AWQ | (none) | Runs with defaults |
| FP8-AWQ | `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` | Disables the DeepGEMM path for this checkpoint |
| MXFP4-AWQ | `VLLM_DISABLED_KERNELS=FlashInferMxFp4LinearKernel` | Disables the FlashInfer MXFP4 linear kernel, so vLLM falls back to `MarlinMxFp4LinearKernel`: 4-bit weights, BF16 activations and BF16 math |

We used the Marlin fallback for MXFP4 because, when we ran these experiments, vLLM's native MXFP4 path on Blackwell (the FlashInfer kernel) wasn't stable enough to run this checkpoint on vLLM 0.24.0.
...
- NVFP4 is the clear throughput winner at every point on the curve. It opens at 2,004 tok/s at concurrency 60 — already above where BF16 ever reaches — and climbs to 3,078.91 output tok/s at no-limit. Its lead over the next-best variant ranges from 608 to 1,020 tok/s, a gap that never closes as load increases.
...
- NVFP4 pushes that cliff furthest out. It holds the lowest TTFT at every concurrency level — 1,132 ms at 360 versus BF16's 8,605 ms (a 7.6× reduction) — and even at no-limit stays at 7.4 s while BF16 is at 38 s, a 5.2× gap. With far more KV cache space and faster 4-bit math, more requests run at once and fewer wait in the queue, so latency degrades gracefully instead of collapsing.
...
- NVFP4-AWQ is the overall winner. It delivers the highest throughput (3,078.91 tok/s, 2.41× BF16's peak) and the lowest latency across the load curve, for only a modest +0.41 PPL. If you are optimizing a serving deployment on Blackwell, this is the default choice.
- FP8-AWQ is the safe pick. Nearly lossless quality (+0.03 PPL) with a solid 1.63× throughput gain — the right call when you want the smallest quality change rather than maximum tokens/sec.
- MXFP8-AWQ is the balanced middle. Slightly better throughput than FP8 with still-tiny quality cost; a reasonable default when you want a bit more speed without moving to 4-bit.
- MXFP4-AWQ is hard to judge from this run. It ran on the Marlin weight-only fallback kernel with BF16 activations, and in that setup it delivered only 1.34× throughput, well behind NVFP4. These numbers measure that kernel, not MXFP4 on Blackwell's FP4 tensor cores.
...
| Use case / Category | Pick | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maximum serving throughput | NVFP4-AWQ | Highest peak output throughput: 3,078.91 tok/s |
| Best latency under load | NVFP4-AWQ | Lowest TTFT / TPOT across most concurrency levels |
| Conservative production quality | FP8-AWQ | Only +0.0299 PPL vs BF16 |
| Best balanced FP8 variant | MXFP8-AWQ | Better throughput than FP8 with a still-small +0.0589 PPL |
| Not measured on its native kernel | MXFP4-AWQ | Ran on the Marlin weight-only fallback; similar PPL hit to NVFP4 but much lower throughput in this run |

If we had to ship one format today for a Blackwell serving workload, it would be NVFP4-AWQ, with FP8-AWQ as the conservative fallback.
...
The experiment set out to answer a simple question: on Blackwell, what do you actually give up when you quantize Qwen3-32B, and what do you get back? The answer is lopsided in the best way — you give up almost nothing on quality and gain a lot on serving performance.

Across every variant, Wikitext perplexity moved by at most +0.44 and GSM8K held steady (even drifting slightly upward, which we treat as noise rather than improvement). Meanwhile, peak output throughput ranged from 1.34× to 2.41× BF16, and time-to-first-token under load improved by up to ~8.4× (NVFP4 vs BF16 at concurrency 420). Quantization on Blackwell is not a quality-vs-size compromise; it is a near-free serving upgrade.

On October 3, 2026, Aleph Alpha posted on X that “Kolibri is here”: seventy-eight billion parameters, three point four six billion active, up to one million tokens of context, “built in Europe,” with weights on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. The same morning the lab published a blog post timed to German Reunification Day and a fifty-page tech report linked from the model card. For readers who follow open weights through Qwen, Mistral, and NVIDIA’s Nemotron lines, the drop can feel abrupt. Aleph Alpha has sold sovereign enterprise AI in Germany for years, but it has not been the default name in the MoE weight wars. Kolibri changes that by publishing a full checkpoint, an inference stack, and tables that compare the model directly to GLM, Nemotron, Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6, Mistral Small, and Gemma variants at roughly three to six billion active parameters per token.
...
The release artifact is Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1 on Hugging Face, dated October 3, 2026. Kolibri is a mixture-of-experts transformer aimed at German and English, with explicit reasoning mode and Hermes-style tool calling. Total parameters are seventy-eight billion; active parameters per token are about three point four six billion, routed across three hundred eighty-four experts per layer with one shared expert and six routed. Weights ship in FP8 blocks with a documented memory footprint near seventy-eight gigabytes, and Aleph Alpha recommends hardware such as two H100s, one H200, or one B200 class GPU for serving.

Context is part of the headline. The model card validates quality up to one million tokens and recommends two hundred sixty-two thousand tokens or less for latency-sensitive or complex production work. Aleph Alpha pre-trained on sixteen-thousand-token sequences, mid-trained on sixty-five thousand, and extended to two hundred sixty-two thousand in a long-context phase, then reports extension without position scaling in sliding-window layers. The X thread’s one-million-token line matches the card, not a rounding error.
...
Aleph Alpha stresses a full training stack rather than a distill-and-release maneuver. The Hugging Face card says pre-training used twenty trillion tokens from a filtered bilingual corpus, roughly sixty-two point five percent English, twenty-three point nine percent German, and thirteen point six percent code, plus mid-training on three point four four trillion tokens and a long-context extension on two hundred one billion tokens. Post-training combined supervised fine-tuning on bilingual open and synthetic data with reinforcement learning across reasoning, agentic, and instruction environments. Compute disclosure on the card lists seven hundred sixty-eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, twenty-one days of pre-training in measured wall time, and additional mid-training and long-context passes on the same cluster class.

The company’s blog describes Kolibri Origin, a thirty-billion-parameter, three-billion-active predecessor with a sixty-five-thousand-token context, as the pipeline proof. Hundreds of ablation runs and automated recovery when hardware or data links failed, in Aleph Alpha’s telling, preceded the larger model. Kolibri Base appears in evaluation tables as the checkpoint post-training starts from, with Kolibri Origin Base as the earlier ablation line. That narrative is how Aleph Alpha answers the “where did this come from?” question: not an overnight download of someone else’s weights, but a second-generation product from a training system the lab had already exercised in public on a smaller bird.
...
The comparative claim lives in Aleph Alpha’s own evaluation appendix on Hugging Face, with a footnote that MoE models are marked against each other while dense models are greyed out because they activate far more parameters per token. Within the three-to-six-billion-active MoE group, Kolibri reports an overall English composite of 75.5 and overall German of 70.8 after post-training. Dense Qwen3.8 27B, outside the MoE comparison set, still shows higher overall composites in the same document at 80.2 English and 79.9 German. Afterimage is reporting Aleph Alpha’s table, not rerunning it. The fair summary is that Kolibri leads the MoE pack on the lab’s chosen averages while stronger dense baselines and individual agent benchmarks remain contested.

Aleph Alpha’s blog frames the same numbers as a Pareto frontier on quality versus decoding throughput per GPU for English and German, arguing no compared post-trained model delivers more benchmark score at the same serving cost. That chart is qualitative packaging on top of the Hugging Face tables. The tech report at aleph-alpha.com/downloads/tech-report.pdf carries architecture detail: fifty-layer MoE, four-to-one sliding-window to global attention, Muon optimizer, and Exact Quantile Balancing across experts.
...
Marketing language on Aleph Alpha’s site ties Kolibri to regulated German and European customers: public administration, industrials, aerospace, on-prem deployment, and supply-chain documentation from data ingestion through evals. That is a different pitch from a Silicon Valley API launch, even though the license is permissive. Apache 2.0 means weights are yours to host; the lab also ships an `aleph-alpha-inference` vLLM plugin and container image for reasoning and tool parsers.

On agentic coding tasks in the same document, Qwen still wins some rows. On dense models with more active parameters per token, Qwen3.8 27B remains ahead on overall averages. candidates.audience_pain: Running out of memory for long contexts, high inference costs, slow performance due to KV cache bottlenecks.
candidates.why_now: Multiple new research papers and releases (TurboQuant, TaSQ, Glyd v0.28.0, GLM-5.3-Flash) are advancing practical KV cache compression, offering significant memory and speed benefits.
candidates.hook_seed: 1-bit KV cache: huge context, tiny memory.

candidates.topic: Agentic RAG for Superior Multi-hop Reasoning
candidates.angle: Agentic RAG loops and agentic retrieval systems, like those using LangChain and Amazon Bedrock, are demonstrating significantly higher accuracy (e.g., 92.7% on Google FRAMES) compared to traditional RAG pipelines by planning retrieval and iterative reasoning for complex multi-hop queries.
candidates.audience_pain: Traditional RAG struggles with complex, multi-document, or multi-hop questions, leading to inaccurate or incomplete answers.
candidates.why_now: New benchmarks and framework integrations (LangChain, Bedrock, GraphRAG combinations) are validating the superior performance of agentic RAG.
candidates.hook_seed: Agentic RAG beats basic RAG: here's why.

candidates.topic: Vulkan for Quantized LLM Inference on Edge Devices
candidates.angle: llama.cpp's new Vulkan-based sparse flash attention mode for quantized key/value data enables faster GPU-accelerated inference, lowering compute costs for running LLMs on edge devices.
candidates.audience_pain: Struggling to run LLMs efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware, seeking ways to optimize inference speed and reduce costs on local GPUs.
candidates.why_now: The latest llama.cpp update specifically adds Vulkan support for quantized K/V, directly addressing edge device optimization.
candidates.hook_seed: Run LLMs faster on edge with Vulkan.

candidates.topic: Open-Source Agent Harnesses for Local AI Development
candidates.angle: Tools like DeepSeek Harness v0.2 and Earendil's Pi 1.0 are providing open-source agent harnesses with official desktop apps, built-in tools, plugin management, and crash-resumable features, making local AI agent development more accessible and robust.
candidates.audience_pain: Difficulty in building, testing, and deploying AI agents locally, lack of integrated tooling for agentic workflows.
candidates.why_now: Recent 1.0 and v0.2 releases of prominent open-source agent harnesses offer mature features for developers.
candidates.hook_seed: Build agents locally: new open-source tools.

candidates.topic: AI's Capability in Designing Its Own Hardware and Materials
candidates.angle: Recent breakthroughs demonstrate AI agents like Opus 5.5 discovering room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates and even developing their own inference hardware (e.g., openTPU).
candidates.audience_pain: Understanding the bleeding edge of AI's autonomous capabilities and its long-term implications for future infrastructure.
candidates.why_now: Multiple reports highlight AI systems moving from software design to physical discovery and hardware architecture.
candidates.hook_seed: AI designs chips. Yes, real inference hardware.

candidates.topic: Accurate Benchmarking for AI Inference Optimization
candidates.angle: Effective benchmarking, measured in milliseconds, is crucial for truly understanding and optimizing AI inference performance, especially with new models like Reflection's Beam achieving similar benchmarks to larger models with 3-4x less compute, or TurboQuant delivering 8x speedups in attention computation.
candidates.audience_pain: Difficulty in accurately measuring and comparing real-world AI inference performance, leading to suboptimal deployment choices and unexpected costs.
candidates.why_now: The increased focus on model efficiency and hardware-specific optimizations (e.g., NVIDIA B200, H100) necessitates precise benchmarking strategies.
candidates.hook_seed: Benchmark milliseconds: true AI inference speed.

candidates.angle: The 'Dust' research explores novel methods for pretraining Transformers entirely without traditional backpropagation, a fundamental shift that could significantly reduce computational complexity and memory requirements during the training phase.
candidates.audience_pain: High computational cost and memory demands associated with training large Transformer models using traditional backpropagation methods.
candidates.why_now: A new research paper ('Dust') on Hacker News is presenting a radical alternative to current Transformer pretraining paradigms.
candidates.hook_seed: Training Transformers without backprop? Dust shows how.

candidates.topic: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) for Stable GPU Infrastructure
candidates.angle: NVIDIA's AICR v1.0 provides open, stable, and verifiable recipes for GPU cluster configuration, offering version-locked, validated component combinations and deployment artifacts to ensure consistent and reliable AI infrastructure.
candidates.audience_pain: Managing complex GPU clusters, ensuring compatibility between software and hardware, achieving stable and verifiable deployments.
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA's release of AICR v1.0 establishes a stable compatibility contract, making it a reliable solution for infrastructure operators.
candidates.hook_seed: Managing GPU clusters? NVIDIA has a stable fix.
